session.title: Taylor's theorem: derivative matching plus a legal remainder
session.focus: Turn a derivative-matching polynomial into a theorem-level local approximation with the Lagrange remainder and all interval/derivative hypotheses visible.
session.purpose: Prevent Taylor polynomials from becoming unexplained formulas by showing exactly what theorem connects them to the target function and where the unknown remainder point comes from.
session.centralCapability: Reconstruct and audit the one-variable Lagrange-remainder theorem on a bounded interval, including its hypotheses and the role of the intermediate point.
session.principalObstacle: The coefficient derivatives are evaluated at the center, which tempts a learner to put the remainder derivative there too; the theorem instead uses an unknown point between the center and the evaluation point and requires derivative hypotheses across that interval.
entryPrerequisites: M12-S02 derivative-matching Taylor polynomial and coefficient rule
requiredOwnership: Reconstruct a valid proof of the degree-2 Lagrange remainder using Rolle/MVT or an equivalent legal argument.
Distinguish the Taylor center from the unknown intermediate remainder point and locate that point between center and evaluation point.
Audit a proposed Taylor-theorem use for the required higher-derivative hypothesis on the whole intervening open interval.
session.applicationScope: One-variable finite-order Taylor theorem on a closed interval joining center and evaluation point; degree-2 proof as representative of the general repeated-Rolle mechanism.
session.transferScope: Changed from theorem reconstruction to hypothesis forensics on a piecewise-smooth function crossing an interior point where the next derivative fails to exist.
inScope: continuous lower derivatives on the closed interval

session.exitCondition: A learner can prove the representative n=2 remainder result and reject the transfer theorem invocation because f''' fails at an interior point, even though the Taylor polynomial at the center exists.
session.lesson:
Orient. A polynomial can match f and its derivatives at a center and still separate from f away from that center. We need a theorem that turns derivative matching into a statement about the residual.

Define. For center a, let P_n be the degree-n Taylor polynomial and R_n(x)=f(x)-P_n(x). If f has n continuous derivatives on the closed interval joining a and x and f^(n+1) exists at every interior point, then for some c strictly between a and x,
R_n(x)=f^(n+1)(c)(x-a)^(n+1)/(n+1)!.
The point c is supplied by the theorem; it is not automatically a or x.

Connect. S02 forced P_n^(k)(a)=f^(k)(a) for k≤n. S05 supplied Rolle/MVT. Those two facts are exactly the ingredients used in the remainder proof.

Explain the proof architecture on degree 1, not on the fixed Main instance. Fix a≠x and choose M so
f(x)-P_1(x)=M(x-a)^2.
Set g(t)=f(t)-P_1(t)-M(t-a)^2. Then g(x)=0, while derivative matching at a gives g(a)=g'(a)=0. Rolle applied to g between a and x gives an interior point d with g'(d)=0. Applying Rolle to g' between a and d gives c strictly between a and x with g''(c)=0. Since g''(t)=f''(t)-2M, we obtain M=f''(c)/2 and hence
f(x)-P_1(x)=f''(c)(x-a)^2/2.
The general theorem repeats the same zero-forcing idea enough times; Main asks you to reconstruct the next degree rather than copy this proof verbatim.

Worked example. Let f(t)=ln t, center a=1 and evaluate x=1.2. For n=1, P_1(t)=t-1 because f(1)=0 and f'(1)=1. Since ln has the required derivatives on [1,1.2], Taylor's theorem gives
ln(1.2)-0.2=f''(c)(0.2)^2/2
for some c∈(1,1.2). Since f''(c)=-1/c^2, the remainder is negative. We have not yet replaced c by a numerical bound; S07 will do that.

Guided practice. For f(t)=e^t, center 0 and a first-degree polynomial evaluated at x=0.3, write only the legal Lagrange-remainder statement and locate c. Check: e^0.3-(1+0.3)=e^c(0.3)^2/2 for some c∈(0,0.3). Do not set c=0 merely because the polynomial coefficients use derivatives at 0.

Distinction check. "P_n uses derivatives at a" and "the remainder contains f^(n+1)(c)" are different theorem roles. Existence of the Taylor polynomial at one point is not enough to invoke the Lagrange theorem across an interval where the next derivative fails.

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-M@1.prompt: Let a<x. Suppose f,f',f'' are continuous on [a,x] and f''' exists at every point of (a,x). Let P_2(t)=f(a)+f'(a)(t-a)+f''(a)(t-a)^2/2. Prove that there is some c∈(a,x) such that f(x)-P_2(x)=f'''(c)(x-a)^3/6. You may use the Rolle/MVT bridge already established in this module. Your proof must make clear why c lies between a and x and must not assume c=a.

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-T@1.prompt: Let f(t)=|t|^3, take center a=-1/2 and evaluation point x=1/2, and consider the degree-2 Taylor polynomial at a. A proposed solution says: “The degree-2 Taylor polynomial exists at a, so Taylor's theorem guarantees c∈(-1/2,1/2) with f(x)-P_2(x)=f'''(c)(x-a)^3/6.” Audit this claim. Compute the needed derivatives on t<0 and t>0, identify the theorem hypothesis that fails, and use the actual remainder together with the possible values of f''' where it exists to show concretely that this invocation cannot be correct.

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-M@1.reference: Set M=[f(x)-P_2(x)]/(x-a)^3 and g(t)=f(t)-P_2(t)-M(t-a)^3. Then g(x)=0 by the definition of M. Taylor matching at a gives g(a)=g'(a)=g''(a)=0. Apply Rolle's theorem to g between a and x to obtain a first point where g'=0; apply it again to g' between a and that point to obtain a point where g''=0; apply it once more to g'' to obtain c∈(a,x) with g'''(c)=0. Since P_2'''=0 and d^3[M(t-a)^3]/dt^3=6M, g'''(c)=f'''(c)-6M=0. Thus M=f'''(c)/6 and f(x)-P_2(x)=f'''(c)(x-a)^3/6. An equivalent correct proof using the established MVT/Rolle machinery is acceptable.

rubric.criterion: Constructs a valid auxiliary/repeated-Rolle (or mathematically equivalent) proof setup in which the residual vanishes at both endpoints and has the needed derivative matching at a.
Legally applies Rolle/MVT successively under the supplied interval hypotheses to obtain an interior c with the required third-derivative relation.
Computes the third derivative of the auxiliary relation correctly and obtains the factor 3!=6.
Concludes the stated remainder formula and explicitly keeps c between a and x rather than replacing it by the center.

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-M@1.marking: Score the public proof obligations, not a preferred notation. Accept any valid proof of this n=2 Lagrange remainder using the established support theorem. Do not require the exact auxiliary-function symbol g or exact order of exposition.

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-T@1.reference: For t>0, f(t)=t^3, so f'(t)=3t^2, f''(t)=6t and f'''(t)=6. For t<0, f(t)=-t^3, so f'(t)=-3t^2, f''(t)=-6t and f'''(t)=-6. At t=0, f'' is continuous with value 0, but f''' does not exist because the one-sided third derivatives are -6 and 6. Since 0 is an interior point of (-1/2,1/2), the n=2 Lagrange theorem's requirement that f''' exist throughout the intervening open interval fails. The degree-2 Taylor polynomial at a=-1/2 still exists: f(a)=1/8, f'(a)=-3/4, f''(a)=3, so at x=1/2 (where x-a=1), P_2(x)=1/8-3/4+3/2=7/8. Thus the actual remainder is 1/8-7/8=-3/4. Wherever f''' exists in the open interval, f'''(c)/6 is either -1 or 1, never -3/4. Hence no legal c can satisfy the claimed formula: existence of P_2 at the center did not establish the theorem's interval hypothesis.

rubric.criterion: Computes the piecewise derivatives sufficiently to show f'''=-6 for t<0, f'''=6 for t>0, and f''' does not exist at the interior point 0.
Identifies failure of the next-derivative hypothesis on the full open interval between center and evaluation point, rather than claiming the Taylor polynomial itself does not exist.
Computes P_2(1/2)=7/8 and the actual remainder -3/4.
Shows the proposed Lagrange form would yield only ±1 for f'''(c)(x-a)^3/6 where f''' exists, so it cannot equal -3/4.

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-T@1.marking: Accept equivalent piecewise-derivative notation and exact fractions/decimals. The key distinction is that P_2 exists at a while the interval theorem is illegal. Do not award the hypothesis criterion for merely saying the function is 'not smooth' without locating the failed derivative.

main.reason: The lesson teaches the repeated-Rolle proof architecture on the distinct degree-1 case; Main reconstructs the degree-2 proof, so the demand is proof reconstruction without exact worked-answer exposure.

transfer.reason: Transfer changes from proving the theorem under supplied legal hypotheses to auditing a piecewise-smooth function that has a valid degree-2 polynomial at the center but fails the next-derivative condition at an interior point, then requires a numerical contradiction witness.

main.wrongApproach: Quote f(x)=P_2(x)+f'''(a)(x-a)^3/6 because all Taylor coefficients are evaluated at a.
main.result: Fails the proof obligations and illegally replaces the theorem's intermediate c by a; cannot earn rows 1,2 or 4.
main.validAlternative: A correct Cauchy-MVT or equivalent Rolle-based proof is accepted even if it does not use the exact g/M notation.

transfer.wrongApproach: Claim the theorem applies because f,f',f'' exist at the center and P_2 can be computed there.
transfer.result: Misses the interval-wide f''' hypothesis and contradicts the explicit remainder values; loses the hypothesis/contradiction criteria.
transfer.validAlternative: Any correct derivative audit that locates nonexistence of f''' at 0 and demonstrates incompatibility with the actual remainder passes.

separation.main: general degree-2 proof with symbolic a,x
separation.finding: No fixed task reuses the worked-example or guided-practice instance. Main reconstructs the next-degree theorem architecture rather than copying the lesson's degree-1 proof; Transfer changes object surface and demand.
